content: 1. HIV prevalence is calculated by determining the proportion of individuals who test positive for HIV among those tested, including those previously known to be HIV-positive. This proportion is then multiplied by 100% to express HIV prevalence as a percentage. 2. When comparing HIV prevalence at specific sites across two surveillance rounds, it is essential to ensure that the sentinel surveillance methods remain consistent between rounds. This allows for valid comparisons of site-level HIV estimates. 3. To assess trends in HIV prevalence over time, surveillance programs can analyze site-level prevalence or median prevalence across sites at national or subnational levels. Consistency in surveillance methods over time is critical for accurate trend analysis. 4. Plotting HIV prevalence over time for specific demographic groups, such as age groups, can help identify changes in infection levels. Graphical methods, such as scatter plots or line graphs, are the most effective way to present trend data, with prevalence estimates on the vertical axis and time on the horizontal axis. At least four rounds of data are recommended for graphical trend analysis. 5. Statistical modeling can also be used to estimate and test trends in HIV prevalence from sentinel surveillance data. This approach is detailed further in Appendix A4. 6. In sentinel surveillance, estimates are representative only of the population accessing the specific antenatal care (ANC) site where the data is collected. Aggregating data to calculate regional or national prevalence estimates is inappropriate unless the sentinel sites are representative of the broader population. 7. Surveillance programs should report the median of site-level prevalence estimates as a summary statistic to minimize the influence of outliers. The range of site-specific prevalence should also be reported to highlight differences between sites. However, the median is not an estimate of national or regional HIV prevalence among ANC attendees. 8. Estimates of HIV prevalence and trends in the general population using data from pregnant women attending ANC should be derived using UNAIDS’ Spectrum analysis tools. 9. Routine program data used for HIV surveillance among pregnant women may include records with missing data. Surveillance programs should establish consistent approaches to handle missing data for analysis. Missing data should be documented, and its limitations on surveillance results should be clearly communicated. 10. Surveillance systems should be continuously monitored and regularly evaluated to ensure reliable data for public health action. Monitoring should focus on elements that affect the reliability of surveillance estimates, such as data quality and HIV testing quality. 11. Underperforming sites, such as those with incomplete data collection or substandard HIV testing, should be identified and targeted for support to improve program services and data quality. If a significant proportion of sites are underperforming, real-time data collection through sentinel surveillance may be considered until routine systems are strengthened. 12. Data completeness and validity should be monitored at the site level. Data are considered complete if they are present and legible in designated fields, and valid if they fall within the expected range of values for each field. 13. Routine data tools used in ANC, such as registers or electronic medical record (EMR) systems, should be monitored to ensure they capture the variables needed for surveillance. Changes to these tools should be planned in collaboration with maternal and child health (MCH) or prevention of mother-to-child transmission (PMTCT) programs to maintain data quality. 14. The quality of aggregate data collected through routine reporting systems depends on both site-level data recording and the transfer and storage of data in above-site repositories. Surveillance programs should work with partners to monitor and improve the quality of these systems. 15. Routine HIV testing at ANC sites, typically using rapid diagnostic tests, is a critical component of surveillance. The quality and accuracy of testing should be supported by a robust quality assurance system, including training, standardized testing practices, and participation in external quality assessment (EQA) programs. 16. Personnel conducting diagnostic testing should maintain standardized records of test kit details, including product names, lot numbers, expiration dates, and individual test results. 17. Quality control specimens, including known HIV-positive and negative samples, should be routinely tested to ensure the accuracy of diagnostic testing. Any incorrect quality control results should be investigated before testing client specimens. 18. Inventory management of test kits is essential to ensure they are used within their shelf lives, stored appropriately, and available in sufficient quantities to avoid compromising the testing algorithm. 19. Syphilis testing quality assurance measures should also be robust and integrated with HIV testing quality assurance systems, as the same principles apply to both. 20. Surveillance programs should interpret HIV surveillance results among pregnant women attending ANC with consideration of representativeness, generalizability, and potential biases in prevalence estimates and trends.
